metadata.description: 'Small vector' optimization: store up to a small number of items on the stack

classification.reasoning: Purpose: The crate is `smallvec`, a very well-known and foundational Rust library providing stack-allocated vectors, with over 1.2 billion downloads, established in 2015, and 83 published versions. Sources/Sinks/Flows: There is no build script (`has_build_script: false`), no network calls, no process spawns, and no file writes. Unsafe blocks are present (42 blocks, 11.76 per KLOC), which is completely normal and expected for a data structure library manually managing heap and stack memory layouts. Anomalies: A false positive on prompt_injection occurred because a code comment containing the word 'Forget' matched a naive pattern. The dependencies (`arbitrary`, `serde`) are standard and expected. Conclusion: The crate is completely legitimate, and no malicious signals are present.

retrieved_context.title: arrayref / internment / append-only-vec trojanized via a malicious dependency (August 2026)
retrieved_context.text: On 2026-08-20, arrayref 0.3.10, internment 0.8.7 and append-only-vec 0.1.9 were published to crates.io from a maintainer account that appears to have been compromised. For arrayref the source was unchanged genuine code; the release added a dependency on the malicious crate proc-macro1. proc-macro1 typosquats proc-macro2 (its library source is a copy, so dependent builds succeed) and forges the real author's name in its metadata; its build.rs reconstructs a base64-encoded URL, downloads an architecture-specific remote binary over TLS with certificate validation disabled, and runs it detached with a command-and-control address as argument, unconditionally on every supported-platform build. internment and append-only-vec added a dependency on an attacker-controlled crate with the same kind of build-script payload. Further crates (aovine, arone, aronenao, proc-macro-en, tinymember) belong to the same campaign; their build scripts were attributed from the campaign rather than analyzed individually. Earlier releases of the trojanized crates are reported as unaffected, and the malicious releases were removed. Lesson: the trojanized crate's own code can be clean; the signal is a NEW dependency whose build script downloads and executes a remote binary.
retrieved_context.source: OSSF malicious-packages MAL-2026-14332 to MAL-2026-14340; SafeDep write-up https://safedep.io/arrayref-proc-macro1-rust-build-time-malware/ ; RustSec advisory-db issue #3161

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: proc-macro compiler-level injection
retrieved_context.text: Procedural macros execute inside the Rust compiler at compile time and can inject arbitrary code into the compiled binary, or exfiltrate the source code being compiled (a trade-secret theft vector distinct from runtime data theft). A legitimate proc-macro's implementation should not need std::net, std::process, or an HTTP client crate -- these are the strongest structural red flags for this attack surface, since a macro's job is token-stream transformation, not network I/O.

retrieved_context.title: CrateDepression / rustdecimal (2022)
retrieved_context.text: A coordinated typosquatting campaign where the crate 'rustdecimal' impersonated the legitimate 'rust_decimal' crate (52M+ downloads at the time). Edit distance from the target name was 1 (removed underscore). The malicious crate's build.rs deployed a Mythic C2 (command and control) agent specifically into GitLab CI/CD pipelines. The payload fingerprinted the environment before activating -- it only deployed inside detected CI systems, evading casual local testing. Attack category: typosquatting + backdoor + CI-targeting build.rs payload.
